parts.label: characterization
parts.text: Isis insists on royal precedence because Tyre's royalty is new and fragile. In the Amarna letters, Tyre's rulers were Pharaoh's vassals: they fell 'seven times and seven times', called him 'my sun', and begged for water and firewood for an island that could not feed itself [2, 3, 8]. Old Egyptian families still remember that. Her generation turned a vassal port into a house that Pharaoh marries as an equal. She holds herself above everyone because one slip would turn her back into the daughter of a servant. Her contempt for common-born Tiye is the scorn she fears from Egypt's own nobles, turned onto someone lower.

parts.label: integration
parts.text: This deepens canon's 'entitled, looks down on Tiye' without changing it, and it explains the trait through Tyre's history rather than through a plot event. It also sets up a quiet parallel: Isis and Tiye are both upstarts in the eyes of the old court.

questions.q: Does Isis know Tyre's vassal past and hide it, or does she believe the house has always been royal?

parts.label: characterization
parts.text: Born around 1205, Isis was a girl on the island when Ugarit and the northern ports fell. Tyre was the coast's harbour-master and took in wrecked ships and their crews [9]. Ugarit's king had sent his army to help the Hittites, and the relief came only after his city had been sacked [15]. Her lesson is that allies arrive late and a city on the sea stands alone. Assyria's raids on the dye coast look to her like the start of Ugarit again. That is why she pushes so hard for Egypt's war: she has seen what happens when a great king decides it is not his problem.

parts.label: integration
parts.text: This gives her war advocacy a personal motive beyond 'my homeland', and it ties her to the Collapse canon. Divergence: Ugarit really fell around 1192–1190 [14], when Isis would be about 13–15. The author can keep that date or shift it a few years so it falls closer to her marriage.
parts.note: ugarit should fall when she was 13-15 not closer to her marriage

questions.q: Did Isis see refugees or a burning city herself, or did she only hear of it through ships and letters?
Was Isis betrothed to Ramesses III before or after the north fell? Was the marriage Tyre's insurance against the fate of Ugarit?

parts.label: plot
parts.text: This flips the Dido legend [32, 33]. When the marriage to the new 20th-Dynasty king was arranged around 1185–1182, Isis had a real claim to rule in Tyre, either jointly with her brother or as their father's favorite. Her brother, or the merchant houses backing him, settled the question by marrying her off to Egypt. Dido had to flee Tyre with the treasure; Isis was sent out of it with a dowry, and nobody had to die. So when the coup catches her in Tyre, she is not a guest but a former rival who has come home, with a son and an Egyptian queen's title, just as Tyre needs someone to lead its war against Assyria.

parts.label: integration
parts.text: Fits the canon that Ramesses III married her to draw northern Canaan back to Egypt: this adds Tyre's own motive for the match. It works whether her brother or a son of hers leads Tyre's war, and it raises the stakes of that open question without settling it.

questions.q: Did Isis agree to the Egyptian marriage as a bargain, or was it done to her?
Does her brother still sit on Tyre's throne in 1160, or has the claim passed to his children?

title: The marriage contract: Great Royal Wife or nothing

parts.label: world
parts.text: Tyre's price for Isis copied Hatti's price for Maathorneferure: she had to be named Great Royal Wife, not one more foreign wife sent to the harem [4]. Her dowry was paid in Tyre's own wealth: dyed purple wool and finished cloth, silver, cedar, and the use of Tyrian ships for Egyptian troops. Egyptian soldiers met her caravan and escorted it down the coast road [4, 2]. She came with a sworn Tyrian household of ladies, scribes who could write Akkadian and Canaanite, and her own priests [5]. That household is a small Tyre inside the khener, with its own budget and its own envoys [6].

parts.label: integration
parts.text: This fits canon: Ramesses III married her to pull northern Canaan back toward Egypt. Divergence: no Levantine city-state ever won Great Royal Wife rank in reality; only great kings like the Hittites did. Her household also gives Isis a ready escort and a route if she is in Tyre during the coup.

questions.q: Did Isis receive an Egyptian court name as Maathorneferure did, or did she insist on keeping her Tyrian name?
Did Ramesses ever send her away to a provincial harem-palace such as Mer-wer, as some scholars think Ramesses II did with his Hittite bride?

title: Partner in the war, not in the bed

parts.label: characterization
parts.text: Isis and Ramesses III do not love each other, but they are real allies. The Assyrian war is the one thing they built together: his legacy and her homeland's safety in one campaign. She thinks secondary wives are beneath jealousy. Her contempt for Tiye is about rank, not the bed, which turns the jealous-first-wife cliché on its head. Like Mantel's Katherine [34], her weapon is never giving ground on titles: she will not address an inferior by a rank she has not granted. What she mourns in the coup is the war they planned more than the man, and Egypt's turn toward an Assyrian marriage is the insult she cannot forgive. That gives her Hecuba's path from grief to revenge [37] without any of her children having to die.
parts.note: she still mourns the man b/c she respects him and did have children with him. and she isnt a warhawk per say but more like she wants to protect her home.

parts.label: integration
parts.text: Consistent with canon: she pushes for the Assyrian war, and her marriage is political. It gives her a personal stake in the planned reversal from war to an Assyrian alliance. It does not touch the open question of where she is during the coup.

questions.q: Did Isis ever love Ramesses III early on, before the partnership became purely political?
questions.answer: she did love him and still loves him. but the love is not from a place of lust or romance

title: Aegon is the evidence against her

parts.label: characterization
parts.text: Isis cannot admit Aegon is unfit, because a failed heir of her blood disproves the creed her pride rests on. So she shields him and blames everyone else: his father's coldness, his companions, the black-market purple trade. Her defense of him is self-defense dressed as a mother's love. This makes Aegon's unfitness, rather than Tiye, the real fault line in her marriage, and it means his eventual growth would vindicate her and humble her at the same time.

parts.label: integration
parts.text: It fits canon: Ramesses III despises Aegon, Aegon must read as clearly unfit, and some of Isis's entitlement shows in her children. It deliberately leaves alone the open question of who dies protecting Aegon.

questions.q: Does Isis know how bad Aegon's purple use is, or does she refuse to know?
questions.answer: she has a pretty good idea

title: She married down, and she knows it

parts.label: characterization
parts.text: Isis's contempt for Tiye's common birth is displaced contempt for her husband's own thin blood. She came from an old, rich house and was given to a usurping general's son, whose claim needed a royal bride and whose throne needed Tyre. She has never let herself say that aloud. The pedestal she demands from everyone, Tiye most of all, is how she proves the bargain was worth making. Every bow from Tiye is a receipt.

parts.label: integration
parts.text: This fits her canon entitlement, her looking down on Tiye, and Ramesses III's distant royal blood. It deepens why her scorn falls on Tiye specifically, without adding events.

questions.q: Does Isis privately consider her own children more royal than their father?

parts.label: characterization
parts.text: Isis believes her house is more royal than her husband's. Tyre's dynasty is old. Ramesses III is the son of a usurping general, 'a second son of a second son of a third daughter.' She married down and knows it, as Olympias carried Achilles's line into Macedon [20]. Her pride is also generational revenge. The palace archive at Pi-Ramesses still holds old Tyrian letters begging pharaoh for water and wood [2, 24], and she never lets anyone forget that Tyre now begs no one. She cannot show contempt for her husband's thin blood, because his legitimacy depends on her. So she turns that contempt on Tiye, whose common birth is a safe target. Her contempt for Tiye is really contempt for the throne she married.

parts.label: integration
parts.text: This fits her entitlement and her scorn for Tiye. It also gives Ramesses III's obsession with legacy a private sting: his own queen outranks him by birth. It also lines Isis up with Tiye in one uncomfortable way, since both married above the throne's own origins.

questions.q: Does Ramesses III know Isis privately looks down on his descent, and does it feed his drive to equal Ramesses II?
Did Isis's children absorb the idea that their Tyrian blood outranks their Egyptian blood?
